claim: White-throated sparrows occur in two alternative plumage morphs: white-striped and tan-striped.
source: White-throated sparrows occur in two alternative plumage morphs, white- and tan-striped (Lowther, 1961).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lowther, 1961.

claim: White-striped birds exhibit increased aggression compared with tan-striped birds.
source: These morphs differ not only in their plumage coloration, but also in their social behavior, with white-striped birds exhibiting increased aggression and more frequent extra-pair copulations, and tan-striped birds engaging in more parental care compared with birds of the white-striped morph (Tuttle, 2003; Maney et al., 2015; Maney, 2008; Horton et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: White-striped birds engage in more frequent extra-pair copulations compared with tan-striped birds.
source: These morphs differ not only in their plumage coloration, but also in their social behavior, with white-striped birds exhibiting increased aggression and more frequent extra-pair copulations, and tan-striped birds engaging in more parental care compared with birds of the white-striped morph (Tuttle, 2003; Maney et al., 2015; Maney, 2008; Horton et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Tan-striped birds engage in more parental care compared with white-striped birds.
source: These morphs differ not only in their plumage coloration, but also in their social behavior, with white-striped birds exhibiting increased aggression and more frequent extra-pair copulations, and tan-striped birds engaging in more parental care compared with birds of the white-striped morph (Tuttle, 2003; Maney et al., 2015; Maney, 2008; Horton et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The alternative morphs are linked to a large (~100 Mbp, >1 k genes) rearrangement on the second largest chromosome, called ZAL2m.
source: These alternative morphs are linked to a large (~100 Mbp, >1 k genes) rearrangement on the second largest chromosome, called ZAL2m, so named because the rearranged chromosome is metacentric.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: White-striped birds are heterozygous for ZAL2m and ZAL2.
source: White-striped birds are heterozygous for ZAL2m and the sub-metacentric chromosomal arrangement, ZAL2, whereas tan-striped birds are homozygous for ZAL2 (30, 31).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (30, 31).

claim: Tan-striped birds are homozygous for ZAL2.
source: White-striped birds are heterozygous for ZAL2m and the sub-metacentric chromosomal arrangement, ZAL2, whereas tan-striped birds are homozygous for ZAL2 (30, 31).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (30, 31).

claim: The supergene is estimated to have arisen 2–3 million years ago.
source: In addition to highly divergent social behavior, this relatively young supergene (estimated to have arisen 2–3 million years ago Tuttle et al., 2016; Thomas et al., 2008; Huynh et al., 2010), is also associated with a remarkable disassortative mating system that maintains the 'balanced' morph frequencies in the population.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tuttle et al., 2016; Thomas et al., 2008; Huynh et al., 2010.

claim: Almost all breeding pairs consist of one bird of each morph.
source: Almost all breeding pairs consist of one bird of each morph, earning the species the moniker 'the bird with four sexes' (Campagna, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Campagna, 2016.

claim: Breeding pairs consisting of two individuals of the same morph are estimated to occur less than 1% of the time.
source: Breeding pairs consisting of two individuals of the same morph are estimated to occur less than 1% of the time (Tuttle et al., 2016; Thorneycroft, 1966) and only six ZAL2m homozygotes (i.e. 'super-white' birds) have ever been identified (Horton et al., 2013; Tuttle et al., 2016; Thorneycroft, 1975; Falls and Kopachena, 2020) out of thousands of birds karyotyped or genotyped.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tuttle et al., 2016; Thorneycroft, 1966.

claim: Only six ZAL2m homozygotes have ever been identified out of thousands of birds karyotyped or genotyped.
source: Breeding pairs consisting of two individuals of the same morph are estimated to occur less than 1% of the time (Tuttle et al., 2016; Thorneycroft, 1966) and only six ZAL2m homozygotes (i.e. 'super-white' birds) have ever been identified (Horton et al., 2013; Tuttle et al., 2016; Thorneycroft, 1975; Falls and Kopachena, 2020) out of thousands of birds karyotyped or genotyped.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Horton et al., 2013; Tuttle et al., 2016; Thorneycroft, 1975; Falls and Kopachena, 2020.

claim: ZAL2m exists in a near-constant state of heterozygosity.
source: Given that ZAL2m exists in a near-constant state of heterozygosity, it is in a state of suppressed recombination, similar to the Y and W sex chromosomes in mammals and birds, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the rarity of ZAL2m homozygotes and the disassortative mating system.

claim: The suppression of recombination on ZAL2m is expected to reduce the efficacy of natural selection, leading to reduced genetic diversity and the degeneration of the chromosome.
source: The suppression of recombination on ZAL2m is expected to reduce the efficacy of natural selection, leading to reduced genetic diversity and the degeneration of the chromosome (Barton and Charlesworth, 1998; Charlesworth, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barton and Charlesworth, 1998; Charlesworth, 2012.

claim: Tuttle et al., 2016 found a weak signal of excess non-synonymous polymorphism for genes inside the rearranged region on ZAL2m.
source: However, Tuttle et al., 2016 found a weak signal of excess non-synonymous polymorphism for genes inside the rearranged region on ZAL2m and reduced allelic expression for ZAL2m genes, which could be consistent with functional degradation of ZAL2m (Tuttle et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tuttle et al., 2016.

claim: Sun et al., 2018 found a slightly higher number of non-synonymous substitutions on ZAL2m compared with ZAL2.
source: (Sun et al., 2018) similarly found a slightly higher number of non-synonymous substitutions and an increased ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous substitution rates (dN/dS) on ZAL2m compared with ZAL2.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2018.

claim: Sun et al., 2018 found reduced expression of ZAL2m alleles in brain tissue.
source: (Sun et al., 2018) also found reduced expression of ZAL2m alleles in brain tissue, perhaps suggesting that the accumulation of deleterious mutations has led to reduced expression of genes from ZAL2m.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2018.

claim: Allelic differences in the promoter region of ESR1 are likely to alter expression.
source: There is already some evidence that this variation affects behavior; allelic differences in the promoter region of the gene encoding estrogen-receptor alpha (ESR1) are likely to alter expression (Merritt et al., 2020), and the expression of this gene was shown to be necessary for aggressive behavior typical of the white-striped morph (Merritt et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Merritt et al., 2020.

claim: The expression of ESR1 is necessary for aggressive behavior typical of the white-striped morph.
source: There is already some evidence that this variation affects behavior; allelic differences in the promoter region of the gene encoding estrogen-receptor alpha (ESR1) are likely to alter expression (Merritt et al., 2020), and the expression of this gene was shown to be necessary for aggressive behavior typical of the white-striped morph (Merritt et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Merritt et al., 2020.

claim: ZAL2m is associated with differential expression of vasoactive intestinal peptide.
source: ZAL2m is also associated with differential expression of a key neuromodulator, vasoactive intestinal peptide (Horton et al., 2020), known to be causal for aggression in songbirds (Goodson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Horton et al., 2020.

claim: Vasoactive intestinal peptide is known to be causal for aggression in songbirds.
source: ZAL2m is also associated with differential expression of a key neuromodulator, vasoactive intestinal peptide (Horton et al., 2020), known to be causal for aggression in songbirds (Goodson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Goodson et al., 2012.

claim: White-striped birds were sequenced at higher coverage than tan-striped birds (average mean depth coverages were 41.5 × vs 28.4 ×).
source: White-striped birds, which are heterozygous for the rearrangement (ZAL2/2m), were sequenced at higher coverage than tan-striped birds (ZAL2 homozygotes) so that we could obtain sufficient reads to separate ZAL2 and ZAL2m alleles in white-striped individuals (average mean depth coverages were 41.5 × vs 28.4 × for white- and tan-striped birds, respectively, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and Supplementary file 2.

claim: A total of 11,382,994 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were discovered.
source: Genomic variants were called according to the guidelines of Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) (ver. 4.1) (Materials and methods), leading to the discovery of a total of 11,382,994 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).
evidence: The claim is supported by data generated in this study.

claim: A significantly higher number of polymorphic sites were found within white-striped birds than tan-striped birds exclusively for ZAL2/2m chromosomal regions.
source: We found a significantly higher number of polymorphic sites within white-striped birds than tan-striped birds exclusively for ZAL2/2m chromosomal regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nucleotide diversity of the rearranged region of the ZAL2/2m chromosomes was elevated in white-striped birds compared with tan-striped birds.
source: Nucleotide diversity of the rearranged region of the ZAL2/2m chromosomes was elevated in white-striped birds compared with tan-striped birds, suggesting distinctive patterns between the two plumage morphs (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The first principal component (PC1) explained 6.7% of the variation in the data and clearly separated tan- and white-striped birds.
source: The first principal component (PC1), which explained 6.7% of the variation in the data, clearly separated tan- and white-striped birds, with the lone super-white individual (ZAL2m/2m homozygote) as a clear outlier.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from principal component analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The super-white individual was a clear outlier in the principal component analysis.
source: The first principal component (PC1), which explained 6.7% of the variation in the data, clearly separated tan- and white-striped birds, with the lone super-white individual (ZAL2m/2m homozygote) as a clear outlier.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from principal component analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tests for admixture failed to identify significant population substructures by geographical origin of samples.
source: Tests for admixture also failed to identify significant population substructures by geographical origin of samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The total assembly size of the super-white bird genome was 1058 Mbp with an N50 length of 3.1 Mbp.
source: The total assembly size was 1058 Mbp (N50 length of 3.1 Mbp, longest scaffold 27 Mbps), comparable to that of the ZAL2/2 reference assembly (1052 Mbp, N50 scaffold length of 4.86 Mbp, longest scaffold 45 Mbp) (see Supplementary file 3 for more details).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the genome assembly presented in the manuscript.

claim: There were 160 putatively ZAL2m-linked scaffolds with a total length of 110.99 Mbp.
source: There were 160 putatively ZAL2m-linked scaffolds (Materials and methods), with a total length (110.99 Mbp) comparable with that of ZAL2-linked scaffolds from the reference assembly (108.5 Mbp Tuttle et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the genome assembly presented in the manuscript.

claim: The average length of the individual ZAL2m-linked scaffolds was significantly shorter than scaffolds on other chromosomes in the super-white assembly (p<0.001).
source: Despite this similarity in total length, however, the average length of the individual ZAL2m-linked scaffolds was significantly shorter than scaffolds on other chromosomes in the super-white assembly (p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the genome assembly data.

claim: The ZAL2m chromosome contained more repeat elements and was especially enriched for long terminal repeat elements (2.4 Mbp vs 2.1 Mbp) and interspersed repeats (5.8 Mbp vs 5.5 Mbp), compared with the ZAL2 chromosome.
source: We found evidence that the ZAL2m chromosome contained more repeat elements and was especially enriched for long terminal repeat elements (2.4 Mbp vs 2.1 Mbp) and interspersed repeats (5.8 Mbp vs 5.5 Mbp), compared with the ZAL2 chromosome.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from repeat element analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: ZAL2 and ZAL2m had accumulated a higher proportion of structural variants (insertions and deletions) compared with other chromosomes.
source: Additionally, we found that ZAL2 and ZAL2m had accumulated a higher proportion of structural variants (insertions and deletions) compared with other chromosomes (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The total number of genetic variants was approximately 12-fold reduced on the ZAL2m alleles compared with ZAL2 alleles (29,420 vs 367,466 SNPs and 3,921 vs 32,479 indels).
source: We found that the total number of genetic variants was approximately 12-fold reduced on the ZAL2m alleles compared with ZAL2 alleles (29,420 vs 367,466 SNPs and 3,921 vs 32,479 indels on ZAL2m and ZAL2, respectively, after excluding singleton variants).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from variant calling analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mean nucleotide diversity was reduced on the ZAL2m chromosome compared with the ZAL2 chromosome (0.0104% vs 0.1141%).
source: The mean nucleotide diversity was similarly reduced on the ZAL2m chromosome compared with the ZAL2 chromosome (0.0104% vs 0.1141% for ZAL2m vs ZAL2, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from nucleotide diversity analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous fixed differences inside the rearranged region was slightly, but significantly, elevated for ZAL2m-derived compared with ZAL2-derived fixed differences.
source: The ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous fixed differences inside the rearranged region was slightly, but significantly, elevated for ZAL2m-derived compared with ZAL2-derived fixed differences (Figure 2c), which is consistent with either positive selection or inefficient purifying selection on ZAL2m.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous nucleotide diversity (πN/πS) was significantly increased on ZAL2m compared with ZAL2 (p=1.3 × 10–13).
source: We found that the ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous nucleotide diversity (πN/πS) was significantly increased on ZAL2m compared with ZAL2 (p=1.3 × 10–13, Mann-Whitney U-test, Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The proportion of Ne between ZAL2m and ZAL2 is 0.12 (±0.01), which is threefold lower than the expected ratio of 0.33.
source: The proportion of Ne between ZAL2m and ZAL2 is 0.12 (±0.01), which is threefold lower than the expected ratio of 0.33 (because the ZAL2m chromosome is 1/3 as frequent as the ZAL2, given 'balanced' morph frequencies observed in the wild).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and inference from nucleotide diversity ratios.

claim: Reduced expression of the ZAL2m alleles was found in 8/10 types of tissue.
source: As predicted and consistent with what was previously reported (Sun et al., 2018), we found evidence of consistently reduced expression of the ZAL2m alleles in 8/10 types of tissue (Figure 2g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2g and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: Allelic bias in gene expression was associated with the rate of non-synonymous fixed differences (X2(1)=9.97, p=0.00159).
source: We found evidence that allelic bias in gene expression was associated with the rate of non-synonymous fixed differences (X2(1)=9.97, p=0.00159), although the effect size was exceedingly small (marginal r2=0.0020) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Neither the rate of synonymous fixed differences nor the number of fixed differences within 1 kb upstream of the transcription start site were associated with allelic bias.
source: Neither the rate of synonymous fixed differences (X2(1)=1.0098, p=0.315, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) nor the number of fixed differences within 1 kb upstream of the transcription start site (X2(1)=0.8992, p=0.343, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c) were associated with allelic bias.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and 1c.

claim: Nucleotide diversity in ZAL2m across the outlier region was 0.001, which is tenfold higher than the mean nucleotide diversity of ZAL2m and exceeds the nucleotide diversity in the corresponding region within ZAL2 by 3.15-fold.
source: On average, nucleotide diversity in ZAL2m across this region was 0.001, which is tenfold higher than the mean nucleotide diversity of ZAL2m and even exceeds the nucleotide diversity in the corresponding region within ZAL2 by 3.15-fold.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from nucleotide diversity analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ZAL2m outlier region includes at least 15 protein-coding genes that are well conserved as single copy genes across 13 avian species.
source: This region, henceforth referred to as the ZAL2m outlier region (Figures 2 and 3), includes at least 15 protein-coding genes that are well conserved as single copy genes across 13 avian species (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 2 and Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The phylogenetic tree of the ZAL2m outlier region exhibited the same topology as those from other regions of the ZAL2m, providing no support for introgression.
source: To first examine whether this region has recently experienced an introgression event that could have caused the observed patterns, we constructed a phylogenetic tree of this region. The resulting tree exhibited the same topology as those from other regions of the ZAL2m, thus providing no support for introgression (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Sliding window estimates of the D-statistic did not show any differences in patterns between haplotypes, suggesting that the multiple haplotype structures in ZAL2m were not introduced by gene flow from Harris' sparrow or from the ZAL2 chromosome.
source: Sliding window estimates of the D-statistic did not show any differences in patterns between haplotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the multiple haplotype structures in ZAL2m were not introduced by gene flow from this closely related species or from the ZAL2 chromosome.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tajima's D was significantly higher throughout the ZAL2m outlier region compared with the genomic background (p<0.001).
source: Tajima's D was significantly higher throughout the ZAL2m outlier region compared with the genomic background (p<0.001, permutation test) (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Two major putative haplotypes were identified in the ZAL2m outlier region, consisting of 17 and 30 ZAL2m chromosomes, respectively.
source: Notably, we identified two major putative haplotypes, which we refer to here as 1 and 2, consisting of 17 and 30 ZAL2m chromosomes, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from haplotype analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The genetic differentiation between the two ZAL2m outlier haplogroups was lower than the differentiation between either haplogroup and ZAL2.
source: The genetic differentiation between the two ZAL2m outlier haplogroups was lower than the differentiation between either haplogroup and ZAL2 (Figure 3d), indicating that the haplogroups have evolved since the split between ZAL2 and ZAL2m.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The sequencing depth for the two haplogroups did not differ significantly (p=0.78).
source: Note that the sequencing depth for the two haplogroups did not differ significantly (p=0.78, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ZAL2m outlier regions exhibited an excess of non-synonymous SNPs compared with synonymous SNPs.
source: The ZAL2m outlier regions exhibited an excess of non-synonymous SNPs compared with synonymous SNPs (Figure 2d), as well as an excess of intermediate frequency minor alleles (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Neither geographic location of collection nor sex was associated with any distinct patterns by haplogroups in a PCA analysis using genetic variants in the region.
source: Neither geographic location of collection nor sex was associated with any distinct patterns by haplogroups in a PCA analysis using genetic variants in the region (Figure 3—figure supplement 5; although note the breeding location of the birds from two of the locations was unknown).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: White-striped birds with the H1 vs the H2 versions did not differ significantly in aggressive behavior, gonad size, tarsus length, cloacal protuberance volume, or any other measure when using the Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing.
source: White-striped birds with the H1 vs the H2 versions did not differ significantly in aggressive behavior (measured during simulated territorial intrusions), gonad size, tarsus length, cloacal protuberance volume, or any other measure when using the Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing to avoid false positives (more than 50 tests were performed).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of phenotypic data.

claim: The gene GREB1 was more highly expressed in haplogroup 2 (unadjusted p=0.0195) in AMV.
source: We found that the gene GREB1 (growth regulating estrogen receptor binding 1) was more highly expressed in haplogroup 2 (unadjusted p=0.0195) in AMV.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data analysis.

claim: There was a trend for the gene KCNS3 to be more highly expressed in both Hyp (unadjusted p=0.0511) and AMV (unadjusted p = 0.1567).
source: Additionally, there was a trend for the gene KCNS3 to be more highly expressed in both Hyp (unadjusted p=0.0511) and AMV (unadjusted p = 0.1567).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data analysis.

claim: KCNS3 encodes a voltage-gated channel subunit that in humans and mice is specific to fast-spiking parvalbumin (inhibitory) neurons.
source: This gene encodes a voltage-gated channel subunit that in humans and mice is specific to fast-spiking parvalbumin (inhibitory) neurons (Georgiev et al., 2014; Miyamae et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Georgiev et al., 2014; Miyamae et al., 2021.

claim: 216 20 kB regions on ZAL2 exhibited a significantly elevated H-statistic (empirical p-values <0.05).
source: We identified 216 20 kB regions on ZAL2 exhibiting a significantly elevated H-statistic (empirical p-values <0.05), which is a measure of the average length of the stretches of linkage disequilibrium between the haplotypes (Schlamp et al., 2016; Messer Lab — Resources, 2014, Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from H-scan analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: There were 68 genes located in regions with a significant (p<0.05) H-statistic for ZAL2m and 109 genes in regions with a significant H-statistic for ZAL2.
source: Overall, there were 68 genes located in regions with a significant (p<0.05) H-statistic for ZAL2m and 109 genes in regions with a significant H-statistic for ZAL2 (Supplementary file 5), meaning that these genes are inside regions showing evidence of a selective sweep.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from H-scan analysis presented in the manuscript and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Among the genes that were differentially expressed between morphs, more of these genes are located inside the rearranged region on ZAL2/2m than expected by chance.
source: First, we found that among the genes that were differentially expressed between morphs, more of these genes are located inside the rearranged region on ZAL2/2m than expected by chance, pointing toward cis- (as opposed to trans-) regulatory differences underlying morph differences in expression (X2 tests showed highly significant effects for both brain regions in adults and nestlings of both sexes, with false discovery rate, FDR, correction to account for the multiple statistical comparisons performed using the Benjamini-Hochberg correction) (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Differential expression significantly predicted the degree of allelic bias in expression of that gene (X2(2)=664.16, p<2.2 × 10–16).
source: Consistent with what we previously reported using only males (Sun et al., 2018), we found that differential expression significantly predicted the degree of allelic bias in expression of that gene (X2(2)=664.16, p<2.2 × 10–16, controlling for sequencing batch and brain region, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Tan-biased genes showed greater ZAL2 allelic bias and white-biased genes showed greater ZAL2m allelic bias than did genes that were not differentially expressed between morphs.
source: In addition, tan-biased genes showed greater ZAL2 allelic bias and white-biased genes showed greater ZAL2m allelic bias than did genes that were not differentially expressed between morphs (post-hoc T>W vs T=W: z=–16.87; post-hoc W>T vs T=W: z=19.63, p<2.2 × 10–16; post-hoc W>T vs T>W: z=26.35, p<2.2 × 10–16) (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The ZAL2m H-statistic was a significant, positive predictor of bias in brain gene expression toward the ZAL2m allele (X2(2)=40.17, p=1.893 × 10–9; t=5.114, p=3.24 × 10–7).
source: For the ZAL2m chromosome, we found that the ZAL2m H-statistic was a significant, positive predictor of bias in brain gene expression toward the ZAL2m allele, controlling for sequencing batch and brain region (X2(2)=40.17, p=1.893 × 10–9; t=5.114, p=3.24 × 10–7) (see Materials and methods) (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Genes that exhibited evidence of positive selection on ZAL2 showed allelic bias toward the ZAL2 allele (X2(2)=24.231, p=5.475 × 10–6; t=–3.151, p=0.00164).
source: Likewise, we found that genes that exhibited evidence of positive selection on ZAL2 showed allelic bias toward the ZAL2 allele (X2(2)=24.231, p=5.475 × 10–6; t=–3.151, p=0.00164) (Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The strongest enrichment for genes was found in the categories 'behavior' (pFDR = 0.0252) and 'metabolic process' (pFDR = 0.0252).
source: Using this set of 409 unique genes, we found the strongest enrichment for genes in the categories 'behavior' (pFDR = 0.0252) and 'metabolic process' (pFDR = 0.0252).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: 205/409 (50.1%) of candidate genes were involved in the broad category 'metabolic processes' (pFDR = 0.0210).
source: Additionally, there was enrichment for several gene ontology categories related to metabolism, with 205/409 (50.1%) of these candidate genes involved in the broad category 'metabolic processes' (pFDR = 0.0210).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Significant enrichment was found in the category 'regulation of multicellular organismal process' (pFDR = 0.0342).
source: We also found significant enrichment in the category 'regulation of multicellular organismal process' (pFDR = 0.0342).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: 97/359 (27.8%) genes exhibiting a signal of allelic bias showed a bias toward the ZAL2m allele.
source: We found that 97/359 (27.8%) genes exhibiting a signal of allelic bias showed a bias toward the ZAL2m allele.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Four genes showing allelic bias toward ZAL2m also overlapped regions exhibiting a significant H-statistic on ZAL2m: PDSS2, XRN2, RPS27A, and TCTE1.
source: Four of those 97 genes also overlapped regions exhibiting a significant H-statistic on ZAL2m: PDSS2 (all trans-polyprenyl-diphosphate synthase), XRN2 (5'–3' exoribonuclease 2), RPS27A (Ubiquitin-40S ribosomal protein S27a), and TCTE1 (T-complex-associated-testis-expressed 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Of the 409 genes that exhibited evidence either of allelic bias or positive selection, 55 exhibited evidences of both.
source: Looking at our results from a different perspective, of the 409 genes that exhibited evidence either of allelic bias or positive selection (by the H-statistic), 55 exhibited evidences of both.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Three genes were located in areas of elevated H-statistic on both the ZAL2 and ZAL2m chromosomes: PDSS2, ATP6V1C2, and GHRL1.
source: Three of these genes were located in areas of elevated H-statistic on both the ZAL2 and ZAL2m chromosomes: PDSS2, ATP6V1C2 (ATPase H+Transporting V1 Subunit C2), and GHRL1 (Grainyhead Like Transcription Factor 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Recombination has not entirely ceased on ZAL2m.
source: Regardless, the degeneration is weak at most, and it appears that recombination has not entirely ceased on ZAL2m.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the linkage disequilibrium decay pattern shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Low level of recombination on ZAL2m likely occurs in rare ZAL2m homozygotes.
source: It is likely that this low level of recombination occurs in rare ZAL2m homozygotes (Horton et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and supported by a citation to Horton et al., 2013.

claim: Complex phenotypes including alternative plumage morphs and life history strategies can evolve prior to the cessation of recombination and despite substantial genetic degeneration.
source: Therefore, the case of the ZAL2m supergene illustrates that complex phenotypes including alternative plumage morphs and life history strategies, can evolve prior to the cessation of recombination and despite substantial genetic degeneration.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Allele-specific gene expression in the brain was associated with signatures of positive selection on both the ZAL2 and ZAL2m chromosomes.
source: We also found that allele-specific gene expression in the brain was associated with these signatures of positive selection on both the ZAL2 and ZAL2m chromosomes, suggesting that this selection has acted on regulatory regions of genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Signatures of balancing selection were discovered maintaining two long-range haplotypes within the ZAL2m supergene.
source: Remarkably, we also discovered clear signatures of balancing selection maintaining two long-range haplotypes within the ZAL2m supergene.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Similar long-range haplotypes have not been previously reported for non-recombining chromosomal polymorphisms.
source: We were surprised by this finding, as similar long-range haplotypes have not, to our knowledge, been previously reported for non-recombining chromosomal polymorphisms.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Balancing selection may function to maintain genetic variability in the face of reduced recombination.
source: Our results suggest that balancing selection may function to maintain genetic variability in the face of reduced recombination, and we might expect to see other instances of balancing selection within supergenes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: GREB1 in mammals is a downstream target of ERα.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gegenhuber et al., 2022.

claim: ERα is causally related to the behavioral differences between morphs in white-throated sparrows.
source: This finding is notable because, in white-throated sparrows, ERα is causally related to the behavioral differences between morphs (Merritt et al., 2020; Horton et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Merritt et al., 2020; Horton et al., 2014.

claim: The ZAL2m supergene is an active arena of multiple evolutionary forces.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that the ZAL2m supergene is far from a degenerating counterpart of a 'normal' autosome. Rather, it is an active arena of multiple evolutionary forces.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Although degeneration is operating on ZAL2m, dynamic selective forces are occurring simultaneously, producing divergent complex phenotypes.
source: Our results show that although degeneration is operating on ZAL2m, dynamic selective forces are occurring simultaneously, producing divergent complex phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: A total of 931,424 SNPs and 97,375 insertions and deletions (InDels) were obtained between ZAL2 and ZAL2m chromosomes.
source: Following this procedure, we obtained a total of 931,424 SNPs and 97,375 insertions and deletions (InDels) between ZAL2 and ZAL2m chromosomes, increasing the number of putatively fixed SNPs between the two chromosomes beyond previous publications (Tuttle et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2018).
